slides.title: Install Spyder and run a traceable .py workflow
slides.subtitle: Meeting B · setup, interface, code cells, Variable Explorer, debugging, and first evidence
slides.teaching: State that today ends with a saved, rerunnable .py file—not merely a successful installation.

outcomes.head: Install
outcomes.body: Choose the supported course installation path and verify the Python environment.

outcomes.head: Navigate
outcomes.body: Identify the Editor, IPython Console, Variable Explorer, Files pane, and working folder.

outcomes.head: Run

items: Install or verify the course environment

slides.teaching: Explain that students who are already installed should complete the verification checklist rather than waiting.

slides.title: The Spyder workflow grows by adding one responsibility at a time

tiers.task: Assign length_m = 7.0 and width_m = 5.0, calculate area_m2, and run from the top.
After area_m2 = 35.0, change length_m to 8.5 without recalculating area. Predict the stored area.
Repair room = Studio, calculate 8.5 × 5.2, restart the kernel, and rerun the complete file.

slides.teaching: Use this slide as the handout map: Easy proves the environment, Medium exposes program state, and Hard combines debugging with reproducibility. Students should not skip the restart-and-run-all check.

slides.title: An IDE bundles the tools you need in one place
slides.definition: Integrated Development Environment: one application that bundles a code editor, a running Python process, and tools for inspecting what that process holds. Spyder is the IDE used all semester. An IDE changes how much of the work you can see; it does not change what Python means.

example.head: Without an IDE vs. with Spyder
example.body:
Without: a plain text editor in one window and a separate terminal in another, with no easy way to see variable values as you go.

With Spyder: write, run, and inspect in one window — Editor, Console, and Variable Explorer together.

slides.note: Python, the IDE, and the libraries you import are three separate things. Removing Spyder would not remove Python.
slides.teaching: Ask who has used a plain text editor before. Contrast switching between separate windows with Spyder showing everything at once. Preview that Editor, Console, and Variable Explorer are each introduced in detail later this session.

slides.title: A stable environment is part of reproducibility
slides.statement: The same script can behave differently when the interpreter, packages, or working folder change.
slides.supporting: Environment: the Python interpreter plus the installed libraries used to run the file. Record it, keep course files together, and verify dependencies before changing code.
slides.teaching: Define environment in plain language: the Python interpreter plus installed libraries used to run the file.

slides.title: Use one supported environment for the whole semester

left.head: Course environment
left.body: Install Miniforge, then create arc500-f26 from the supplied ARC500_environment.yml. Conda keeps the compiled scientific and geospatial packages compatible across the semester.

right.head: Spyder application
right.body: Install Spyder with its official standalone installer, then open a console in arc500-f26. Do not install course packages into Spyder’s internal environment from the IPython Console.

slides.teaching: Show the two separate objects: the Spyder application and the arc500-f26 interpreter. Current Spyder 6 guidance recommends an external Conda environment when specialized packages are needed.

slides.title: Create, connect, and verify in four checkpoints

steps.label: INSTALL
steps.head: Get Miniforge + Spyder
steps.body: Download each from its official project page; accept the platform defaults.

steps.label: CREATE
steps.head: Build arc500-f26
steps.body: Create it from the supplied course environment file.

steps.label: CONNECT
steps.head: Choose the environment
steps.body: In Spyder 6, select arc500-f26 for a new console.

steps.label: VERIFY
steps.head: Run the preflight
steps.body: Continue only when the final line says ARC500 PREFLIGHT: PASS.

slides.teaching: Demonstrate the Windows path. Verbally note that macOS/Linux use a terminal. Keep the complete commands in the installation guide, not on the projected slide.

slides.title: These libraries form the semester toolchain
slides.callout: The shared environment installs the complete toolchain once. A successful preflight is evidence that the interpreter—not just the Spyder window—can support the course.
slides.teaching: Distinguish Python itself, the IDE, and imported libraries. Students often treat these as one object.

slides.title: Checkpoint 1: prove the environment works
slides.prompt: Open Spyder in arc500-f26 and verify the environment before editing the handout.
steps: Run ARC500_environment_preflight.py from a terminal.
Open a Spyder console in arc500-f26 and run the file again.
Confirm the executable path names the course environment.
Continue only after the final line reads ARC500 PREFLIGHT: PASS.
slides.teaching: Circulate with a two-column roster: terminal preflight passed; Spyder preflight passed. Do not troubleshoot by changing several installation methods at once.

slides.title: Spyder keeps authoring, state, and evidence visible
slides.editorText:
# %% first cell
length_m = 6.0
width_m = 4.0
area_m2 = length_m * width_m
slides.explorerText:
area_m2   24.0   float
length_m   6.0   float
width_m   4.0   float
slides.teaching: Point to each pane and ask what evidence it supplies. The Editor stores the procedure; Variable Explorer exposes state; Console displays interaction and output.

slides.title: Name the Python role before pressing Run
rows: a value written directly in code
a name that refers to a value
code that evaluates to a value
binds a name to the right-side result
asks a reusable procedure to run
slides.callout: Spyder helps you inspect these ideas, but it does not change their Python meaning.
slides.teaching: Adapted from FS25 L3. Point to the Editor, Variable Explorer, and Console as students identify each term.

slides.title: The Editor holds one file; # %% divides it into cells
slides.definition: A cell marker. To Python it is only a comment, ignored at run time. To Spyder it marks where one runnable chunk of the file ends and the next begins, so Ctrl+Enter can run a few lines at a time instead of the whole script.

example.head: # %% room-area checkpoint
example.body:
The Editor holds the saved .py file: its cells, its comments and assumptions, the complete rerunnable sequence, and text you can search and revise.

Words after the marker name the cell, so one file reads as a sequence of checkpoints.

slides.note: One file tells one coherent story. Cells create checkpoints, but the script must still run from top to bottom after a restart.
slides.teaching: Show that # %% is a comment to Python but a cell marker to Spyder. Delete the marker live and show that the code still runs — only the cell divisions disappear.

slides.title: The Console records execution history

left.head: Useful evidence
left.body:
Printed output from print()
Warnings and error messages
Interactive checks typed at the prompt
The numbered In and Out history

right.head: Important limitation
right.body: The console remembers earlier objects. Code may appear to work because a value survives from an old run — or may fail because a name from a deleted line is still there. Restart periodically and run from the top.

slides.teaching: Demonstrate a name that exists in the console even after its assignment line is deleted from the Editor.

slides.title: The kernel is the Python process that remembers
slides.definition: The running Python process behind the Console. It executes whatever you send it and keeps every name you create until you restart it. Deleting a line in the Editor does not remove the name that line already created.

example.head: Consoles → Restart kernel
example.body: Restarting discards every variable and every import, then hands back an empty Console. Run the file again from the top: any name that only survived from an older run now fails, which is exactly the evidence you want.

slides.note: Two students can run identical files and see different results if one has a kernel still holding names from an earlier attempt.
slides.teaching: Restart live, rerun one cell, and let the class watch a name disappear from the Variable Explorer. Name this as the reason restart-and-run-all is a verification method, not a superstition.

slides.title: Variable Explorer makes program state inspectable

left.head: Inspect
left.body:
Name — what you called it
Type — the kind of value it holds
Value — what it holds right now
Shape or size — for larger objects
Changes — after every cell you run

right.head: Do not rely on it alone
right.body: A visible value can still be wrong: right number, wrong unit; right unit, wrong assumption. Pair inspection with comments, units, predicted results, assertions, and independent calculations.

slides.teaching: Have students locate a variable and say its name, value, type, and unit aloud.

slides.title: A project folder keeps relative paths portable

steps.label: FOLDER
steps.head: Create one module folder
steps.body: Keep the handout, data, and outputs under one Week 01 folder. Confirm it also appears in Spyder's Files pane, which mirrors your file system.

steps.label: SAVE
steps.head: Save the .py file
steps.body: Use a descriptive filename before the first run.

steps.label: SET
steps.head: Choose working folder
steps.body: Working folder (or working directory): the folder Python checks first for relative file paths. Point Spyder to your module folder, not Downloads or an old project.

steps.label: CHECK
steps.head: Confirm with Path.cwd()
steps.body: Print the current path and verify that required files exist.

slides.teaching: Show why an absolute path copied from one laptop is not reproducible.

slides.title: The working directory is where relative paths start
slides.definition: The folder Python treats as “here” while your code runs. A relative path such as 'rooms.csv' is looked for inside it. Spyder shows the current one in the toolbar and in the Files pane — and it is not automatically the folder your .py file was saved in.

example.head: Path.cwd()
example.body:
Prints the folder Python is actually using. Compare it with where the handout is saved before blaming the code for a file it cannot find.

The box in Spyder's toolbar sets it, and the Files pane then lists that folder's contents.

slides.note: An absolute path typed from your own laptop breaks on someone else's. Set the working directory, then keep paths short and relative.
slides.teaching: Open Spyder's working-directory box and change it live, then rerun Path.cwd(). Ask which of the two folders on screen Python is actually using.

slides.title: import brings in code someone else already wrote
slides.definition: A module is a file of pre-written Python code with a name, such as sys or pathlib. A library such as NumPy or pandas is a published collection of modules. import loads a module into the kernel so its tools become available by name.

example.head: import sys
example.body:
Loads the whole module. Call its tools through the module name: sys.version.

from pathlib import Path takes one tool out of its module, so you call Path.cwd() directly — no module name in front.

slides.note: import does not download anything. The module must already be installed in the environment, which is what the check cell proved.
slides.teaching: Point back to the toolchain table: NumPy, pandas, and the rest are imported the same way, all semester. Ask why 'from X import Y' saves typing compared to 'import X'.

slides.title: Read an import line from left to right

parts.label: Where it lives
parts.body: Names the module you are reaching into for one tool.

parts.label: The module
parts.body: A standard-library module for working with file paths.

parts.label: The action
parts.body: Loads it now, in this kernel, at this line — not before.

parts.label: The one tool
parts.body: Only this name arrives; call it with no prefix.

slides.teaching: Read the line aloud in English: from the pathlib module, import the tool named Path. Then contrast with 'import sys', where nothing is singled out and every tool keeps its sys. prefix.

slides.title: Print the environment before trusting it
slides.code:
from pathlib import Path
import sys

print('Python:', sys.version.split()[0])
print('Executable:', sys.executable)
print('Working folder:', Path.cwd())
slides.explainBody: sys and pathlib are two standard-library modules (previous slides). The executable identifies which Python runs the file; the working folder controls relative file paths. Record both instead of guessing.
slides.teaching: Students run this cell and compare their path with the folder containing the handout.

slides.title: Use cells as a repeatable verification cycle

steps.label: READ
steps.head: Read the cell
steps.body: Identify inputs, created names, and expected output.

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.head: Predict first
steps.body: Write the value, type, or error you expect.

steps.label: RUN
steps.head: Execute the cell
steps.body: Ctrl+Enter runs the current # %% cell inside the kernel—the running Python process that holds your variables between runs.

steps.label: VERIFY
steps.head: Inspect evidence
steps.body: Check console output, Variable Explorer, and any assertions.

slides.teaching: Demonstrate Ctrl+Enter. Explain that F9 runs selected lines but should not replace coherent cells.

slides.title: Your first saved program creates named evidence
slides.code:
# %% room-area checkpoint
room_name = 'Gallery'
length_m = 8.5
width_m = 5.2
area_m2 = length_m * width_m

print(room_name)
print(area_m2)
slides.explainBody: Before running, state every name and expected value. After running, confirm output and types. Save the file, restart the kernel, and run the cell again.
slides.teaching: Use this as the guided demonstration before students modify their handout.

slides.title: Studio 1: establish a clean project
slides.prompt: Create a Week 01 module that another student could run without editing paths.
steps: Save the student .py file inside the module folder.
Run the environment and working-folder check.
Add your name and one architectural interest to the opening output.
Restart and run the first two cells again.
slides.teaching: Check file location, not just printed output. Students should be able to close and reopen the module without losing the workflow.

slides.title: Which value does area_m2 still hold?
slides.code:
length_m = 8.5
width_m = 5.2
area_m2 = length_m * width_m

width_m = 6.0
print(area_m2)
slides.question: What does the last line print?
slides.why: 51.0 assumes line 3 is a live formula. It stored one value; changing width_m afterwards leaves it alone.
slides.teaching: Take a show of hands before revealing. Most rooms split between 44.2 and 51.0 — the 51.0 vote is the spreadsheet habit, where a cell recalculates when its input changes. Option D is the restart superstition: restarting and rerunning this file still prints 44.2, because file order, not kernel history, decides. Option C ('an error') is the belief that reassigning width_m retroactively invalidates area_m2, the way a spreadsheet flags a broken reference — Python assignment is a one-time snapshot, not a standing rule it keeps enforcing. Do not correct anyone verbally; run it, then open the Variable Explorer.

slides.title: Changing one name does not recalculate another
slides.code:
length_m = 8.5
width_m = 5.2
area_m2 = length_m * width_m

width_m = 6.0
print(area_m2)
slides.explainBody: area_m2 keeps the earlier result. Changing width_m does not automatically rerun the prior assignment. Rerun the calculation cell or structure the script so dependencies execute in order.
slides.teaching: Step through with the Variable Explorer open: width_m changes to 6.0 in the table while area_m2 sits unchanged at 44.2. Then rerun the assignment line to show 51.0 appear.

slides.title: Studio 2: trace values through cells
slides.prompt: Predict every value before running the next cell.
steps: Complete the supplied trace table for length, width, and area.
Run one cell and compare the Variable Explorer with the table.
Change width_m without rerunning area; explain the stale result.
Restart and run from the top to restore a coherent state.
slides.teaching: The goal is understanding program state, not memorizing a shortcut. Ask each pair to explain why restart-and-run-all is a verification method.

slides.title: What does a bare word on the right side do?
slides.code:
room = 'Studio'
length_m = 10
width_m = five
area_m2 = length_m * width_m
print(area_m2)
slides.question: What happens when line 3 runs?
options: the script runs; print fails instead
slides.why: A bare word is a name lookup, not text. Quotes would make it text; five was never assigned, so line 3 stops.
slides.teaching: Options A and B are the two beliefs beginners actually hold: that Python reads the word as text, or that it understands the English number. Option D is the belief that errors surface only where a value is used. Collect votes, then run it.

slides.title: Read a traceback from its final line
slides.code:
room = 'Studio'
length_m = 10
width_m = five
area_m2 = length_m * width_m
print(area_m2)
slides.output:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "week01b_demo.py", line 3, in <module>
    width_m = five
              ^^^^
NameError: name 'five' is not defined
slides.explainBody: A traceback is the block Python prints when it cannot continue; it lists the chain of calls, most specific line last. The carets mark the word that failed. Read the final line, locate the statement, compare intent with syntax, change one thing, and rerun.
slides.teaching: Do not fix the error immediately. Have students identify the category, location, and intended representation. Note that nothing printed: execution stopped at line 3, before print was ever reached.

slides.title: The last line of a traceback names the failure

parts.label: The error type
parts.body: The category of failure. Python names it first.

parts.label: A name lookup
parts.body: Python was resolving a name, not a file or number.

parts.label: The exact name
parts.body: Quoted, so you can copy it into Editor search.

parts.label: Never assigned
parts.body: No line in this kernel ever assigned that name.

slides.teaching: Have students read this line back as one English sentence before touching the keyboard. Then ask the two repair questions: should five have been a number, or should it have been quoted text?

slides.title: Studio 3: repair one defect at a time
slides.prompt: The handout contains syntax, runtime, and modeling defects.
steps: Predict the first failure before running.
Repair only that defect and rerun.
Continue until the program executes, then check the arithmetic model.
Add a comment classifying every repaired defect.
slides.teaching: Expected final rectangular-room area is 50 m². Emphasize that the final modeling error may remain after all Python errors disappear.

slides.title: Audit AI assistance at the point of use

steps.label: PROMPT
steps.head: Preserve the request
steps.body: Record the question and relevant context.

steps.label: COMPARE
steps.head: Inspect the suggestion
steps.body: Compare every line with course concepts and project assumptions.

steps.label: TEST
steps.head: Add evidence
steps.body: Use predicted, known, and boundary cases.

steps.label: DECIDE
steps.head: Accept, modify, or reject
steps.body: State the reason and preserve the final tested version.

slides.teaching: Students fill the AI-use record even when the record states that no generative AI was used.

slides.title: Exit check: prove the workflow is reproducible
slides.prompt: Demonstrate your file from a clean Spyder state.
steps: Save the file and close all open plots or consoles.
Restart the IPython kernel.
Run the complete file from the top.
Show the expected output, final variables, and AI-use record.
slides.teaching: Use a peer check: one student narrates while the other verifies the saved file, clean restart, output, and explanation.

slides.title: The IDE supports evidence—not understanding by itself
takeaways: Install one stable course environment and verify its interpreter.
Use Editor, Console, and Variable Explorer for different forms of evidence.
Treat # %% cells as checkpoints inside one complete script.
Restart, rerun, inspect, test, and document assistance.
slides.teaching: Collect the environment check and one-sentence reflection: which Spyder pane gave the most useful evidence today?
